mo_d_red_dihedral_wall.blurb: A short bolted wall on the north side of Robinson Bluff, the second face you reach after turning left at the foot of the stairs. It was the first wall equipped here and makes a natural opening stop. Thirteen sport lines run about 50 feet, starting with an easy one and finishing around 5.11. The bulk sit in the 5.10 range, with a few in the 5.7 to 5.9 bracket for warming up, so it suits a mixed group. Practice rappel anchors at the left end give newer climbers a place to learn. The namesake dihedral at 5.9 is a local benchmark for that grade.

mo_drive_in_the.blurb: A small sport-climbing section of Capen Park in Columbia, tucked beside Hinkson Creek. About a dozen bolted lines are split between a couple of short walls, and the grades are friendly: mostly 5.6 to 5.8, a handful at 5.10, and a single 5.11 for anyone wanting a harder tick. Summer visitors can find some shade here. It is a quick stroll from the main lot, over the old bridge and along the quarry road to a steep trail down toward the water, which makes it a good after-work stop and a gentle place to lead your first bolted routes.

mo_1_burns_side.blurb: The first wall you meet when walking in at Monegaw Springs in western Missouri, recognizable by its large cave. The sandstone here is steep and roofed, and the twelve lines are almost all bolted sport routes with one boulder problem. This is not a beginner wall: the climbing runs from 5.10 up through 5.12, with an even split between the 5.10s, 5.11s and 5.12s. A defined trail leads west from the parking area, so you reach the rock quickly, and the area also holds one very long multipitch sport line for those wanting a bigger day.

mo_crescent_wall.blurb: Crescent Wall is the first sector north of the main walk-down at Trapper's Camp, a river-side limestone bluff outside Osceola. The face is a slab joined to a vertical buttress, with good rock on most lines and some weaker patches. Twelve routes mix traditional and bolted climbing, so bring a rack as well as quickdraws. Most grades fall in the 5.9 to 5.10 band, with one easy line, one 5.7, and a few stiffer 5.11 to 5.13 challenges. The bluffs here face west and carry little afternoon shade, and high water can reach the base.

mo_chubb_trail_crack_wall.approach: Follow the Chubb Trail east on foot or by bike to mile marker 4, then turn south onto a faint path that climbs a steep, rocky bank to the base of the wall. Stay off the railroad tracks.
mo_chubb_trail_crack_wall.blurb: A pocketed limestone wall beside the Chubb Trail, west of St. Louis near the Meramec River. A long crack that takes gear well splits the face, with bolted lines on either side. Most of the twelve routes are sport, plus a trad line, an aid line and a pair of boulder problems. Grades are modest: mostly 5.8 to 5.10, so it works for newer leaders and for people looking for a quick top-rope session. Several lines start with bouldery moves. The trees along the railroad give summer shade, and the walk in is short enough to do by bike.
